title: Work-Energy Theorem
body:
The **work-energy theorem** states that the net work done on an object equals its change in
kinetic energy.

$$
W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}mv_i^2
$$

It converts a force question into an arithmetic one whenever the question asks about speed and
says nothing about time.

```
A 10 kg block at 5 m/s slides to a stop against friction of 29.4 N. How far?

  ΔKE = 0 - ½(10)(5²) = -125 J
  W = -f·d = -29.4 d
  -29.4 d = -125     ->     d = 4.25 m
```

No time appeared anywhere, and neither did the acceleration, which is the advantage over
[[Newton's Laws]] applied directly. The theorem also handles a force that changes with
position, since [[Work]] is an integral in that case, where the kinematic equations would fail.

It holds for every force, conservative or not, which is what separates it from
[[Conservation of Energy]]: the theorem accounts for friction by counting its
negative work, where energy conservation has to add a loss term.
